chapter_theme: The teacher's sermon to Neelakesi finishes the account of suffering in the four states of birth (beasts killed by nature, war, hunt, sacrifice and medicine; humans pained by their own passions or by harms from elements, beings and disease; even the gods coming to an end), then offers its cure: the threefold medicine of knowledge, clear faith and conduct, with the Jain means of knowledge, the limbs of right faith and the grades of conduct, ending in heaven and then release.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break

104.reading: The teacher goes on with the suffering of beasts: they wander ruined by cold heavy rain, are driven into battle to die of wounds, are chased and tormented for the sake of food, and lose their lives in countless nets.
104.nuance: Most of the harms listed are done by humans (war, the hunt, the net), so the account of the beast's state of birth is also a charge against those who use and kill animals; it leads straight into the next verse's list of killings.

claims.claim: birth as a beast is full of suffering from weather, war, hunting and the snare

105.reading: He adds the deaths beasts suffer when Vedic ritualists offer them in sacrifice, when base men kill them for spirits and gods, and when they are prescribed to be fed as medicine for named diseases: the sufferings that come by death are many.
105.nuance: The verse names the Vedic ritualists (வேதவாதியர்) and their sacrifice outright and counts it from the victim's side, as one more way a beast dies in pain. The Vedic answer is not given here; the charge is argued out with the Vedic disputant in the Veda debate (836-839), where the killing for gods and ancestors is said to bind the killers.

claims.claim: killing animals in Vedic sacrifice, for spirits and gods, or as medicine inflicts the suffering of death on them

106.reading: Addressing her, the teacher says that the suffering humans undergo among the four trembling states of birth is of two parts: what falls to those who lack self-restraint, and what is common to all.
106.nuance: நாற்கதி, the four states of birth (hell, beast, human, god), is the frame of the whole sermon; this verse moves from the beasts of 104-105 to humans and introduces the division that 107-115 work out.

claims.claim: of the four states of birth, the human's suffering is partly the fruit of lacking restraint and partly common to all

107.reading: The pains of the unrestrained are the gateway of evil deeds, the mind's fault of hatred, anger with pride and deceit, attachment, grief and fear: all of these are the sufferings of those who lack restraint.
107.nuance: Anger (வெகுளி), pride (மானம்), deceit (மாயம்) and attachment (பற்று) together match the four passions that Jain teaching names as the binders of karma; the verse treats them not only as causes of later pain but as present pain. The reading of line 3's பற்று as greed or attachment is mine.

claims.claim: anger, pride, deceit and attachment are themselves the suffering of the unrestrained, as well as the door to evil deeds

108.reading: Men do not reckon that it will drive them into an evil state of birth, do not care that their noble lineage will be stained, do not see that it is a cover filled with swarms of worms, and so perish for the sake of a filthy body, alas.
108.nuance: Desire is not named; the object is only அழுக்குடம்பு, the filthy body, and the verse is in the list of the sufferings of the unrestrained, so lust is the likely sense. It sets three deterrents side by side: the next birth, the family's name, and disgust at the body.

claims.claim: ruin for the sake of the impure body leads to an evil rebirth and stains one's lineage

109.reading: Then the common affliction: it divides into two, harm from outside (இடையூறு), which itself branches into two, and bodily disease, which opens into three.
109.nuance: The sermon now classifies suffering as a physician classifies diseases; the scheme of 109-113 is what the remedy in 116 answers.

claims.claim: suffering common to all is of two kinds, harm from outside and disease of the body

110.reading: He names the two outside harms as those that come from what has life and from what lacks it, and says the first of them, the lifeless, is the four elements.
110.nuance: Line 3 (அடையா உயிரதுவும் அல்லதுவும்) is compressed; that the 'first' is the lifeless kind rests on 111, which lists the elemental harms and ends உயிரல்ல ஊறே.

claims.claim: harm from outside comes either from living beings or from lifeless things, the four elements

111.reading: Heavy rain and flood, the hurling wind, black rockfall and stone, deadly poison, the many weapons of battle, red fire and thunder striking here: all these are harms that come from no living being.

claims.claim: flood, wind, rockfall, poison, weapons, fire and thunder harm without any living agent

112.reading: Spirits that strike and afflict in their anger, men's lasting killing in many ways, and the harm that comes from cruel beasts: these three alike are harms that come from living beings.
112.nuance: செத்துவங்கள் in line 1 I take as beings or spirits (from sattva) that afflict; the word is rare and the sense is not certain.

claims.claim: spirits, men and beasts are the three living sources of outside harm

113.reading: The bodily diseases are three: those that can be cured, those that by their nature cannot, and those that, unlike the ones that yield to applied medicine, pass away by subsiding.
113.nuance: உவசமம் (line 2) looks like upaśama, quieting; the third class may be diseases that settle of themselves, but the contrast with செய்ம்மருந்தின் ஊர்வனவும் is not clear to me.

claims.claim: bodily diseases are curable, incurable, or such as pass by subsiding rather than by medicine

114.reading: He tells her that even all the gods he described before come at last to an end, and that apart from this they have no great suffering, and turns to the darkness that the wicked, other than her own kind, enter.
114.nuance: The sense of lines 3-4 (நுமர் அன்றிப் பொல்லாதவர்கள் உறும் அல்லை) is unsure: நுமர், 'your people', may be the demons of 115, set apart from the other wicked. The gods' end as their only suffering is the clearest point.

claims.claim: even the gods' heavenly life comes to an end

115.reading: Those like her, he says, make pain like fire for all, are called demons everywhere and do what no one would cherish; if it is she herself, she is not such now, but those like her are.
115.nuance: The teacher turns the account of suffering onto his listener: she was a பேய் who did harm, and the verse marks her change by exempting her from her own kind. The reading of line 4 (நீயே எனின் அல்லை) as 'not you, now' is mine.

116.reading: These are diseases hard to shake off; the medicine fit to cure them is the triple discipline of understanding, clear faith and conduct, and those who take it are not born again into the disease and come to great joy.
116.nuance: The three are the Jain three jewels (right faith, knowledge, conduct), here named திரியோகம் and given as medicine after the classification of disease in 109-113; no god administers them, the soul takes them itself (உண்டார், line 3).

claims.claim: the threefold remedy of knowledge, clear faith and conduct ends the disease of birth and brings great joy

117.reading: Of the three medicines, if she would hear the goodness of knowledge: it is to know well, without defect, the existing realities beginning with the soul; that is its essence.

claims.claim: right knowledge is faultless knowing of the real categories beginning with the soul

118.reading: Means of valid knowledge are perception and what is other than perception; perception comprises knowledge through the five senses and mind, avadhi, the pure manahparyaya and kevala.
118.nuance: Ranking sense-and-mind knowledge under perception together with the three supersensory kinds (clairvoyance, knowing others' minds, omniscience) is how later Jain logicians arranged the means of knowledge; the older Jain scheme put sense knowledge among the indirect kinds. The verse follows the former. Its perception reaches beyond the senses, which rival schools deny.

claims.claim: valid knowledge is perceptual or non-perceptual, and perception includes, beside sense-and-mind knowledge, the supersensory avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala

119.reading: Memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and the scripture spoken by the truthful sages: these five, he says, are the means of knowledge other than perception.
119.nuance: Memory and recognition count here as valid knowledge; schools that treat memory as no means of knowledge would reject that. அணுமை in line 2 is read as inference (அனுமை).

claims.claim: the non-perceptual means of knowledge are five: memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and the word of the sages' scripture

120.reading: Placing, standpoints and the means of knowledge are the doors of entry, and the soul with its qualities is examined through the categories of search; if one enters through these without straying, knowledge rises to incomparable eminence.
120.nuance: வைப்பு, நயன், அளவை and மார்க்கணை look like the Jain technical terms nikshepa, naya, pramana and margana; the line division and syntax of lines 1-3 are hard and the reading is tentative.

claims.claim: the soul and its qualities are to be known through placing, standpoints, means of knowledge and the categories of search

121.reading: The kind of right faith, say the victors, is to hold in mind the eight excellent things beginning with God, an unturning longing for the flood of bliss that spreads and surges: that is clear faith.
121.nuance: The verse cites the victors (வென்றவர், the Jinas) as its authority. Which eight things are meant is not spelled out here.

claims.claim: right faith is unturning trust in the eight things beginning with God, joined to longing for bliss

122.reading: Having escaped the three follies that come first, not praising others for love, fear, desire, the world or the outward sign, and standing free of the eight prides: this is the nature of those who have joyful right faith.
122.nuance: The three follies (மூடம்) and eight prides (மயம்) are standard Jain lists of what spoils faith; line 2's division (உலகோடிலிங் காத்த ரொப்பு) is hard and my reading of it is tentative.

claims.claim: one of right faith is free of the three follies and the eight prides and praises no false object out of love, fear or desire

123.reading: Freedom from doubt, desire, disgust and delusion, removing faults, steadying those who have strayed, love without falsehood and showing the peerless dharma: these eight are the limbs of right faith in hand, and its excellence.

claims.claim: right faith has eight limbs, from freedom from doubt to steadying the wavering, love of fellow believers and spreading the dharma

124.reading: Conduct, say those who know the rule of the victors' books, is that which, one with good faith and knowledge, does not leave the heart; and it is of two kinds, the undiminished and the partial.
124.nuance: The complete and the partial (குன்றாத ஒன்றும் குறைபாட்டதும்) are most likely the full vows of the renouncer and the lesser vows of the householder; the verse itself names only the two grades. Conduct here grows out of faith and knowledge and is not separate from them.

claims.claim: conduct joined to faith and knowledge is either complete or partial

125.reading: Guarding, restraint, forbearance and the other good virtues, the twofold penance taken up with resolve, enduring hardships and all such things: these are the excellence of the conduct that refuses change.
125.nuance: இருசார்வு (line 2) I take as penance of two kinds, outer and inner, and பரிசை (line 3) as the hardships to be borne; மாற்றம் மறுக்கும் (line 4) is unclear, perhaps conduct that admits no turning back.

claims.claim: conduct is shown in restraint, forbearance and the other virtues, twofold penance and the endurance of hardship

126.reading: All souls that take this discipline together, good one, live with the dwellers of the high sky as their kings and enjoy their pleasures, and then, with no unfitting deed clinging to them, join the one good bliss, where there is no loss.
126.nuance: Heaven is a stage, not the goal: the verse puts the gods' pleasures before release and makes release the end of karma's clinging (வினை புல்லல் இன்றி), which 114's word on the gods' end prepares.

claims.claim: those who take faith, knowledge and conduct together pass through heavenly enjoyment and, free of clinging karma, reach the single bliss of release

links.note: The invocation praises the god whose word removes the suffering of souls; the sermon names that word's content as a medicine of three parts the soul takes.
links.teaches: The invocation's claim that the god ends suffering by his word, not by intervening, is made concrete here: the cure is a discipline the hearer takes, so the god's role stays that of teacher.

links.note: The invocation says Neelakesi was a demoness of harm whose heart turned; the teacher, describing demons as fire to all, exempts her from her own kind.
links.teaches: Her conversion is acknowledged inside the sermon itself, which uses her former kind as its example of harm while addressing her as one already changed.

links.note: The sermon lists killing for spirits and gods among the beasts' deaths; in the Veda debate Neelakesi tells the Vedic disputant that killings for the Vasus, Rudras and ancestors bring hard karma on the killers.
links.teaches: The sermon counts the sacrifice from the victim's side and the later debate from the sacrificer's, so the Jain case against the rite is made twice: the beast suffers, and the deed returns on the one who kills.

links.note: The Kural ranks abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Neelakesi lists the Vedic sacrifice among the deaths that make a beast's birth a suffering.
links.teaches: The couplet weighs sacrifice and abstention as merits for the actor and leaves the rite standing as a lesser good; the Jain sermon removes it from the scale of merit by counting it as a harm to the slain beast.

gains.a: the sermon's charge is seen as a sharpening of an older Tamil ranking that already put non-killing above the rite
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown to be open to the harder reading that sacrifice is itself a killing, which a Jain teacher draws

links.note: The Naladiyar's fool hails a pot of filth as a woman because of its skin; the Neelakesi's men perish for a filthy body worm-filled under its cover.
links.teaches: The quatrain rests its case on disgust alone, while the sermon sets the same disgust beside the evil rebirth and the stained lineage, so the impure body becomes one of three reckonings a restrained man makes rather than the whole argument.

gains.a: the sermon's compressed image of the covered body is explained by the quatrain's fuller picture of skin hiding the openings
gains.b: the quatrain's single argument from the body's foulness is placed within a teaching of rebirth and family honour it does not state

links.note: The Kural says pain perishes when the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; the Neelakesi names anger, pride, deceit and attachment as the very pains of the unrestrained.
links.teaches: Both make the passions the root of suffering, but they count them differently: the Kural's three (desire, anger, confusion) against the Jain four (anger, pride, deceit, attachment), so pride and deceit, absent from the couplet, are for the Jain teacher as basic as anger.

gains.a: the Jain list is seen against an older Tamil triad and shows what it adds, pride and deceit
gains.b: the couplet's triad is shown to be one count among rival counts of the passions, not the only Tamil one

links.note: Both call the cure of the soul a medicine that leaves it clear: in the Neelakesi the soul takes the three remedies of knowledge, clear faith and conduct; in Tirumular the mind becomes clear when Nandi gives grace, like a madman cured by medicine.
links.teaches: The shared image of medicine and clarity hides opposed accounts of who heals: for the Jain sermon clarity is one of the remedies the soul swallows itself, for Tirumular it is the effect of the Lord's grace, and on the Jain reading no giver of grace is needed.

gains.a: the sermon's godless remedy is seen as a real alternative to a Tamil account of release by grace that uses the same image
gains.b: the verse's claim that clarity is given, not achieved, is sharpened by a rival who makes clarity something the soul takes

links.note: The Kural tells the healer to find the disease, its source and the means that subdue it; the Neelakesi sermon classifies suffering as disease in 109-113 and then names its remedy.
links.teaches: The sermon follows the physician's order the couplet sets down, diagnosis by kinds before the cure, and applies it to the disease of birth, so the Kural's medical rule serves as the shape of a religious argument.

gains.a: the sermon's long classification of harms is seen to have a purpose, the diagnosis that must precede the remedy
gains.b: the couplet's method is shown at work outside medicine, governing how a teacher reasons about suffering itself

links.note: The Vedic logician in the Manimekalai defines perception as fivefold sense knowledge; the Neelakesi's teacher counts as perception also avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala, knowledge without the senses.
links.teaches: The two epics define the same first means of knowledge incompatibly: for the logician perception ends at the five senses, for the Jain it reaches up to omniscience, which is what lets the Jain claim an all-knowing teacher as a source of valid knowledge.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Vedic logician lists comparison, scripture, presumption and other means beside perception and inference; the Neelakesi's teacher lists memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture.
links.teaches: Both lists keep inference and scripture, but the Jain list admits memory and recognition as valid knowledge and leaves out comparison and presumption, so the count of means is itself a point of difference between the schools the epics stage.

links.note: The Kural asks what a householder living in dharma gains by taking the outside way; the Neelakesi grades conduct as complete or partial.
links.teaches: If the partial conduct is the householder's, as Jain usage suggests, the sermon accepts the household as a path of dharma but ranks it below renunciation, which is just the ranking the couplet's question refuses.

gains.a: the sermon's bare division into two grades is seen to answer a Tamil claim of the householder's equal standing
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown meeting a rival that grants the household dharma yet calls it incomplete

new_concepts.gloss: the sacrifice: the Vedic rite performed by priests for a patron, and by extension a deed spoken of as a sacrifice

source_issues: 119 line 2: அணுமை, read as அனுமை (inference); the ண may be a misprint.
122 line 2: the word division உலகோடிலிங் காத்த ரொப்பு is doubtful and the line hard to construe.
126 line 2: the division மன்ன ரும்மாய் looks wrong (perhaps மன்னரும் ஆய்).
114 lines 3-4 and 120 lines 1-3 are syntactically obscure as printed.
